title: The Evolution of AI in Legal Tech: A Conversation with ContractPodAi's Atena Reyhani
author: Atena Reyhani

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source predicts end-to-end coordination among specialist AI agents and new interfaces for human–AI collaboration, but it does not address whether automation weakens apprenticeship or partner succession, nor does it propose funding, simulation, feedback or broader career paths. Its implications for the expertise pipeline therefore cannot be determined.
qs: So now AI can really analyze the information, outsource and dynamically drive intelligence from it, engage multiple AI agents in the background to really perform a task end-to-end.
That really impacts the user interface that is needed to accommodate this kind of human AI collaboration.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: Reyhani accepts the broader contract-intelligence proposition and materially extends it by connecting contract terms with performance data held in adjacent systems. She proposes agentic retrieval at the source to reduce manual entry and support proactive, cross-system action, while offering expected benefits rather than measured outcomes.
qs: Still, a lot of information that is related to the performance of these terms are in adjacent systems, right?

So we really identified this opportunity to create connected intelligence with these agents that are capable of identifying this information at the source, driving intelligence from it, eliminating the need for manual entry of data.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Reyhani supports the shift from isolated chatbot outputs to coordinated, multistep agentic workflows and retains human direction over goals and decisions. Her account aligns with the cluster’s orchestration and human-intervention themes, but does not substantively address error propagation, verification costs or measured reliability.
qs: Like in that example, you know, you could ask the first agent to start a process, but that agent is going to likely decide that it needs more tools, it needs more agents and, you know, other actions to be done.
There are recommendations that are coming in and there’s the human that makes the decision on what direction to go and asking what needs to be done.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: Reyhani directly supports the cluster’s principal shift from product availability and announcements to the organisational work required to realise value. She emphasises practical alignment, strategic deployment, training and enterprise change management, while offering implementation guidance rather than measured evidence of realised benefits.
qs: And that is, number one, really aligning these capabilities of AI to practical organizations needs and being able to operationalize it at the scale to translate technology to value.
Really a lot of user training that is going to help with user adoption and that change management across enterprise work stream.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Reyhani supports the cluster’s practical-adaptation framing by arguing that access to AI alone does not create value; organisations must align tools with real needs, operationalise them at scale, and provide training and change management. Her view is based on professional judgment rather than measured outcomes and does not directly address information filtering or release chasing.
qs: And that is, number one, really aligning these capabilities of AI to practical organizations needs and being able to operationalize it at the scale to translate technology to value.
Really a lot of user training that is going to help with user adoption and that change management across enterprise work stream.

st.t: Legal platforms: Content and governance differentiate workflows
st.an: Reyhani supports the cluster’s core proposition that enterprise legal-AI value depends on legal-specific models combined with governance and deployment infrastructure, rather than models alone. Her claims about expanded workflows and adoption also fit the cluster’s workflow-integration theme, but she provides no quantified performance evidence and does not address authoritative content or continuing human verification.
qs: And what that means is that we have an ecosystem of expert legal models in the comprehensive solution around it.
That is, you know, the frameworks, the guard rails, the infrastructure innovation, everything that enterprise or organization need and can use to really operationalize AI at a scale.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Reyhani directly supports the cluster’s central proposition by prioritising organisational value, actionable intelligence and workflow redesign over technical capability alone. Her account is experiential and aspirational, however, and does not address lawyer control, verification or measured implementation outcomes.
qs: Now, one of the common themes for success that I see is adding this perspective of value in addition to what are the technology  and what it is and how to use it to the value that it brings to the table and the impact that it makes for our organization.
We are really looking at how we can  and  redefine the way that legal teams work and the enterprise work stream this process, right?

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Reyhani directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that legal AI creates value only through organisational adaptation. She identifies practical alignment, strategic deployment, user training and enterprise change management as necessary implementation conditions, while treating the claims as forward-looking professional judgment rather than measured outcomes.
qs: And that is, number one, really aligning these capabilities of AI to practical organizations needs and being able to operationalize it at the scale to translate technology to value.
Really a lot of user training that is going to help with user adoption and that change management across enterprise work stream.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Reyhani supports selective, human-led deployment: agents may execute connected, multi-step workflows, but humans retain direction and decision authority. She also agrees that value depends on embedding AI in practical workflows and investing in strategic deployment, training, adoption and change management. Her account is more optimistic and vendor-led than the synthesis, with limited independent evidence on capability limits or verification, but it does not conflict with the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: Atena Reyhani (09:05)  Yeah, I think the human is in the loop is going to be as part of that human AI collaboration, right?
And that is, number one, really aligning these capabilities of AI to practical organizations needs and being able to operationalize it at the scale to translate technology to value.

kp.k: Conversational interfaces lower adoption barriers but are only starting points
kp.d: Reyhani explains the prevalence of chat-style legal AI interfaces through intuitive human communication and reduced learning demands. She regards conversational interfaces as an initial design approach rather than the endpoint as products move toward comprehensive task execution; these are product-design judgments, not reported usability study findings.
qs: It reduces that cognitive load for users to really go learn a new user interface to use the technology.
that chat box or conversational user interface is just the beginning. It’s just the starting point, right?

kp.k: Agentic systems could shift conversation toward embedded collaboration
kp.d: Reyhani predicts AI will operate where users already work and move beyond passive chatbot responses into end-to-end workflows. She contrasts traditional platforms' predefined navigation, forms and dashboards with systems that analyze information and coordinate agents dynamically. Word and Outlook are examples raised by Lambert, not specifically identified deployments.
qs: Absolutely, it is definitely going to be where the user is for maximizing that adoption.
I really think that we are going to shift from these simple human AI conversation to more deeper human AI collaboration.
engage multiple AI agents in the background to really perform a task end-to-end.

kp.k: Specialist agents may select tools and coordinate legal tasks
kp.d: Reyhani envisages ecosystems of targeted agents in which an initial agent determines which additional tools, agents and actions are required. Gebauer identifies a potential consequence: users could specify desired outcomes without knowing their organization's available tools; Reyhani agrees. The discussion presents an anticipated workflow, not evidence of measured deployment results.
qs: It’s going to be ecosystem of agents each having very targeted expertise that are going to work together.
you could ask the first agent to start a process, but that agent is going to likely decide that it needs more tools, it needs more agents
they’re not going to have to even know the tools at all because they’ll just say, this is what I want.

kp.k: Human direction and approvals remain within automated workflows
kp.d: Asked about human involvement, Reyhani describes people choosing directions and requesting work while agents analyze unstructured legal and organizational information and take actions. In her account, humans return for approvals or other necessary actions while automatable steps proceed. This is a collaboration model; she does not specify a separate verification protocol for checking AI output.
qs: There are recommendations that are coming in and there’s the human that makes the decision on what direction to go and asking what needs to be done.
And then when it’s needed, bring in the human for approval, bring a human for different actions that are needed but automate what is possible.

kp.k: Contract AI expands into adjacent enterprise legal work
kp.d: Reyhani says ContractPodAi began in contract lifecycle management over a decade earlier and increased investment in its Leah generative AI solution during the preceding couple of years. She describes expansion into compliance, obligation management and entity analysis, supported by models, guardrails and infrastructure intended for enterprise-scale operation. These are the vendor executive's descriptions of product scope and intended benefits.
qs: Now we started our journey over a decade ago in contract lifecycle management space.
specifically in the past couple of years, we strategically increased our investment in our GenAI solution called Leah.
use cases like compliance, obligation management, entity analysis, and many other adjacent use cases that we offer products for.

kp.k: Enterprise buyers and Big Four partners use the platform
kp.d: Reyhani reports use across enterprise legal, procurement and sales processes, alongside use by PwC and KPMG in delivering legal services and offering the software to enterprise organizations. Asked where use is greatest, she answers that it is a combination of internal and client work without quantifying the split. ContractPodAi is described as the software provider, distinct from its legal-service partners.
qs: We have lot of enterprise organizations that are using our products in legal procurement, sales processes.
We also have our partners like PwC and KPMG that are using our product for their legal services in addition to offering our products to their enterprise organizations.

kp.k: Connected contract intelligence targets fragmented data and manual entry
kp.d: Reyhani argues that contract terms and information about their performance reside across adjacent systems, often as difficult-to-access unstructured documents. She describes agents retrieving information at its source, deriving intelligence and enabling proactive action rather than requiring manual entry. Leah's proposed command-center scope includes regulatory requirements, policies, procedures and compliance standards, not merely contracts; improved operations remain an anticipated benefit.
qs: a lot of information that is related to the performance of these terms are in adjacent systems
agents that are capable of identifying this information at the source, driving intelligence from it, eliminating the need for manual entry of data.
command center not only for contracts, but adjacent information that drives decision and intelligence on top of the contracts.

kp.k: Privacy and security are foundational enterprise adoption requirements
kp.d: Lambert raises law firms' security, regulatory and ethical obligations when questioning the platform's document-management scope. Reyhani responds that privacy and security are foundational across enterprise products and says the provider needs infrastructure, models and innovation to guarantee them alongside performance. The discussion supplies no specific security controls, certifications or testing results.
qs: privacy is so important. Security is so important, right?

Those are such a foundational considerations for us as a provider to have the infrastructure, the AI models, the innovations that we need to guarantee the security, guarantee the privacy and the performance for our customers.

kp.k: Entity analysis illustrates work beyond document extraction
kp.d: Reyhani reports that an unnamed large investment firm uses Leah for entity analysis and SEC reporting. She describes evolving interconnected documents, AI understanding information not explicitly stated, and applying processes and algorithms to quarterly entity classification. She contrasts this with previous semi-manual work supported by extraction tools; the account provides neither quantified outcomes nor independent customer evidence.
qs: One of the largest investment firms are now using Leah for their entity analysis and SEC reporting.
Contracts is one part of that, but there are interconnected documents that are ever evolving.
the work was there, it was being done semi-manually, course, extraction tools were there

kp.k: Market conversations return from technology enthusiasm to operational value
kp.d: Reyhani describes customer discussions as value-focused before the generative AI 'moment' two or three years earlier, technology-focused for a year to a year and a half, and subsequently returning to value as the market matures. Her account emphasizes incorporation into organizational work, adoption and scaling, rather than acquiring technology alone. This is a qualitative observation from customer conversations, not a market survey.
qs: before what I call AI moment, two or three years ago when we started talking about Gen.AI
for a year, a year and a half, that was the trend. All we’re talking about is technology, technology, technology.
Not only what is the technology, but what can we do with the technology? How can we incorporate it? How can we operationalize it at a scale?

kp.k: Vertical models and marketplaces could distribute specialist expertise
kp.d: Reyhani identifies a shift from general models toward targeted expert models working together. She describes Leah Marketplace as an initiative under development to systematize contributions from customers, PwC, KPMG and other experts into industry- and subject-specific products. She predicts faster innovation through this marketplace approach, comparing it with Salesforce, Microsoft marketplaces and app stores; no launch date or demonstrated acceleration is supplied.
qs: this transition from general models to really vertical intelligence, like expert and targeted solutions, expert and targeted models that can work together
one of the initiatives that I’m very excited about that we are working on at ContractPodAi is called the Leah Marketplace.
I think of it as crowdsourcing innovation, starting with leaders in the industry.

kp.k: Deployment, training and change management determine practical value
kp.d: Looking to the coming months and years, Reyhani identifies matching AI capabilities to organizational needs and operationalizing them at scale as central challenges. She emphasizes strategic deployment, user training, adoption and enterprise-wide change management, while arguing that lessons from previous digital transformations remain applicable. This concerns organizational technology adoption rather than changes to lawyer qualification or junior-lawyer formation.
qs: really aligning these capabilities of AI to practical organizations needs and being able to operationalize it at the scale to translate technology to value.
Really a lot of user training that is going to help with user adoption and that change management across enterprise work stream.
a lot of those learning still apply to AI and GenAI products.

kp.k: Diverse participation is presented as important for AI innovation
kp.d: Reyhani argues that women bring diverse perspectives crucial to innovation and encourages more active participation in shaping AI. She emphasizes contributions from different professional backgrounds, including outside AI and law. This is a normative view about product development, not a measured finding about workforce composition or innovation outcomes.
qs: As for women in AI, I really believe that we bring in that diverse perspective that is so crucial for innovation.
with different areas of expertise, not necessarily AI, not necessarily even legal
And I encourage more of us to take active role.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Atena Reyhani predicts a shift from conversational interfaces to embedded human–AI collaboration and agent-coordinated, end-to-end legal workflows.
pts.d: Reyhani says familiar conversational interfaces currently lower cognitive load and adoption barriers, but are only a starting point. She predicts tools will move to where users already work and support collaboration rather than merely answering questions. Specialized agents will select other tools and agents, analyze unstructured legal and organizational information, and take actions across negotiation and approval processes. Her framing retains human direction and approvals when needed; it is not a claim that legal work will become wholly autonomous.

pts.k: Reyhani claims AI connects contracts with adjacent business information, reduces manual data entry, and expands automation beyond contract lifecycle management.
pts.d: She describes ContractPodAi's Leah as supporting compliance, obligation management, entity analysis, and other enterprise workflows as well as contracting. She argues that information relevant to contract performance resides in adjacent systems and unstructured documents; agents can identify it at source, derive intelligence, and initiate proactive actions. She predicts smarter, more connected operations and presents this as part of a broader SaaS shift from siloed technologies to agent-enabled platforms. Leah's scope includes company policies, regulatory requirements, procedures, and compliance standards rather than contracts alone.

pts.k: Reyhani says AI now enables complex, interconnected-document analysis that extraction tools alone could not address.
pts.d: Her concrete example is an unnamed large investment firm using Leah for entity analysis and SEC reporting. She describes evolving interconnected documents, inference beyond explicitly stated information, and application of processes and algorithms to classify entities quarterly. She contrasts this with previously semi-manual work supported by extraction tools. This is a reported deployment and capability claim, not a quantified claim about accuracy, cost savings, or complete replacement of human analysis.

pts.k: Reyhani predicts specialized legal intelligence and a partner marketplace will accelerate product innovation.
pts.d: She identifies an emerging move from general models toward expert, targeted models working together within platforms. She describes Leah Marketplace as an initiative under development that would systematically incorporate customer and partner expertise into enterprise legal generative-AI products. She predicts faster innovation through industry-specific and subject-matter contributions, including those of PwC and KPMG. This is a roadmap prediction rather than a reported marketplace outcome.

pts.k: Reyhani says legal-AI purchasing conversations are returning from technology enthusiasm to practical value, with deployment and adoption becoming central challenges.
pts.d: Based on customer conversations, she describes a technology-focused period following the generative-AI surge and a current return to questions about incorporation, scaling, and value. She predicts that matching capabilities to organizational needs, strategic deployment, user training, adoption, and change management will occupy the industry in coming months and years. She argues that lessons from earlier digital transformations remain applicable.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims are supported principally by Reyhani's product-development experience, customer observations, reported deployments, and partner relationships.
pts.d: As ContractPodAi's Chief Product Officer, Reyhani draws on experience across generations of AI and customer deployments. Concrete examples include the unnamed investment firm's entity-analysis and SEC-reporting use, enterprise use in legal, procurement, and sales, and PwC and KPMG using the product in legal services. Her account of changing market priorities rests on customer conversations. Agent-interface evolution and marketplace acceleration are forward-looking arguments informed by product work, not measured findings. The transcript supplies no quantitative performance results, benchmarks, comparative studies, or quantified adoption or savings data.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Reyhani mixes present deployment claims with emerging transitions and undated roadmap predictions; value realization depends on organizational implementation and safeguards.
pts.d: Relative to the interview, she describes enterprise and investment-firm deployments as current and increased GenAI investment as occurring over the past couple of years. She locates the 'AI moment' two or three years earlier, followed by roughly a year to a year and a half of technology-centered discussion. Human–AI collaboration and specialized-agent platforms are developing transitions without fixed completion dates. Leah Marketplace is being worked on, with no launch date stated. Operationalization challenges are expected in coming months and years. Conditions include aligning products to practical needs, training and change management, human direction and approval when needed, and infrastructure supporting privacy, security, and performance.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are enterprise legal teams and adjacent business functions, legal-service providers using the software, and legal-AI product partners.
pts.d: Enterprise legal, procurement, sales, and compliance functions are presented as beneficiaries of simplified contracting, connected information, automation, and enhanced decision-making. Investment firms are a specific segment for entity analysis and regulatory reporting. PwC and KPMG are described as Big Four partners using the software to deliver legal services and offering it to enterprise customers; ContractPodAi itself is the software provider. Users would increasingly specify goals and collaborate with agents, while organizations face deployment, training, and change-management work. Marketplace contributors would bring industry and subject expertise into products. Reyhani does not make concrete predictions here about lawyer headcount, staffing structures, billing models, or access to justice.
